conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been sick for two days—nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. I can’t keep anything down. It’s that gnawing pain right here in my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the pain sharp or more like a constant ache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More of a constant gnawing. It’s epigastric, near my belly button. Not getting worse, but not better either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And the vomiting—any blood or is it just yellow or green?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. It’s yellow-green, kind of bilious. I’ve thrown up over ten times in the last two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the diarrhea—how many times a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More than six times. Watery. I usually have chronic diarrhea, but this is worse than my baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any fevers, chills, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fevers. I feel crummy, but no respiratory symptoms. I was surprised when they told me I have the flu.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your flu test came back positive for Influenza B. That could be contributing to your nausea and GI symptoms, especially since you’re immunosuppressed from your liver transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that could happen. I thought the flu was just cough and fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can affect the gut too, especially in people like you. We’ve started you on Tamiflu—30 mg twice a day, adjusted for your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my other meds? I take a lot for pain and my transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your mycophenolate, prednisone, and pain meds. But we’ve held your loperamide and opium tincture for now—just until we’re sure there’s no infection causing the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, right. Because of the risk of trapping an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve sent stool tests for C. diff, norovirus, and other infections. All came back negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my kidney numbers? I know they’ve been up before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.5, which is a bit higher than your baseline, so we’re watching for acute kidney injury on top of your chronic kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s usually around 1.1. But it’s bounced between 1.5 and 2 before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, so we’ll keep monitoring it daily. We’ve given you 3 liters of IV fluids to help with dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit dry. My mouth’s been parched.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your exam showed dry mucous membranes. We’ll keep you on IV fluids until you can tolerate sips and we’re sure you’re rehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips. If you keep those down, we’ll slowly advance your diet. Nutrition is consulting to help plan your G-tube feeds once you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually rely on the G-tube for most of my calories. But I’m so nauseous, I didn’t think I could handle feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re holding off for now. We don’t want to worsen the nausea. But we’ll reassess daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I kept down some apple juice last night. Still nauseous, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We did an ultrasound of your liver this morning—everything looks stable. Hepatic vessels are patent, no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any sign of bile duct problems or infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bile duct is mildly dilated at 1.1 cm, but that’s unchanged from before. No signs of obstruction or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my CMV? I’ve had colitis from that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV IgM is negative, and viral load is undetectable. No sign of reactivation. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent cultures for salmonella, shigella, campylobacter—all negative. So it looks like viral gastroenteritis, likely from the flu.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no bacteria or parasites?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And your lipase was normal, so we’re not worried about pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I try more food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, let’s try clear liquids and see how you do. We’ll advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs show your white count and hemoglobin are down a bit, but stable. Creatinine is holding at 1.6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. Your pancytopenia is chronic, so this may just be your baseline. But we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on darbepoetin for that. Should I restart it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss with your transplant team. For now, focus on recovering your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had only three bowel movements today. Closer to my usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Since your cultures are negative, we’ll restart your loperamide and opium tincture as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel like I’m turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been tolerating a soft diet, and your vitals are stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home meds, including the Tamiflu for the full 10 days. Restart your G-tube feeds as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pending blood and stool cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those will keep being monitored. If anything comes back positive, we’ll let you know. But so far, everything points to viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I follow up with my transplant doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. And your primary care provider to review your labs and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today. You look much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot better. Still weak, but the nausea is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep taking the Tamiflu, advance your diet slowly, and monitor for any return of symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? Can I go back to my usual doses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your home medications as listed in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.
